title: Beyond Majority Voting: Aggregating LLMs by Trusting the Surprising
one_liner: When asking multiple AI models the same question, ignore majority vote and instead reward models when their answer matches others who rarely agree.
lead: When you ask multiple AI models the same question, the simplest approach is majority voting: count votes and pick the most common answer. But this treats all models as equally reliable, which they are not. Some models are better calibrated (they know when they are guessing), and some models' answers correlate with each other (they make the same mistakes). This paper introduces a training-free method that detects which models tend to agree with the crowd and which stand alone, then reweights their votes so that independent dissenters have more power.

paras: Imagine you ask ten AI models to diagnose a medical image. Five say cancer, four say benign, one abstains. Majority voting picks cancer. But what if those five models are a fine-tuned variant that was trained on biased data? What if the four dissenters are independent models that rarely agree with the first five, yet each time they do, they are right? Majority voting cannot know this.

A beginner might try: just ask each model how confident it is in its own answer. But models often do not know how to calibrate confidence honestly—they confabulate certainty even when uncertain. A more advanced beginner might try to cluster which models agree with each other and downweight the cluster, but without a principled metric, this becomes a guess.

callout.html: Majority voting ignores that models have latent reliability patterns: some are more trustworthy, some correlate with each other, and models that dare to be wrong when others agree often point to a real blind spot.

panels.title: 1. Naive voting
panels.caption: Majority voting: 5 red wins, all models count equally, patterns invisible.

panels.title: 2. Models have latent types
panels.caption: Some models cluster together (hot), others are independent (free). Voting treats them all alike.

panels.title: 3. Measure correlation
panels.viz_args: Count: how often does this model agree with the crowd?
panels.caption: For each model, count how many times it matches the majority consensus.

panels.title: 4. Upweight the surprising
panels.caption: Models that rarely agree with the crowd get boosted. Independence becomes a strength.

panels.title: 5. Better collective decision
panels.viz_args: Weighted vote: the surprises speak louder
panels.caption: Weighted votes now catch when the minority is onto something the majority missed.

steps.text: Ask all models the same question, collect their answers.
For each model, count: how often does it agree with majority consensus? (Popularity score.)
Models that agreed often are downweighted. Models that disagreed often are upweighted. (Inverse Surprising Popularity.)
For the Optimal Weight variant, also measure per-model accuracy on the test set.
Re-aggregate using the learned weights. The final answer is now resilient to correlated errors.

paras: The paper changes the way votes are counted when combining multiple AI model answers. Instead of each model's vote counting equally, each vote is multiplied by a learned weight that depends on the model's historical pattern of agreement with the crowd.

hidden.name: how often a model bucks the consensus
paras: Surprising Popularity is a measurement of whether a model tends to agree or disagree with the majority consensus across many test questions. A model with high popularity has voted with the crowd often (it is a conformist). A model with low popularity has disagreed often (it is a rebel).

The paper estimates this by running all models on a batch of questions and recording, for each model, what fraction of the time it matched the majority answer. If a model matches the majority 95% of the time, its popularity is high. If a model matches only 40% of the time, its popularity is low. The Inverse Surprising Popularity method (ISP) then reverses this: it gives high weight to models with low popularity, treating the rebels as a tie-breaker vote.

heat.caption: Darker means higher popularity (agrees with crowd more often). Highlighted: low-popularity rebels that get upweighted.

reads.html: Think of it like jury deliberation: if juror A always agrees with the room, and juror B always speaks up alone, you might trust juror B's lone dissent more, because when they disagree, they bring new information.

Popularity is measured as the fraction of times, observed in a holdout test set, that each model agreed with the majority label. ISP assigns weights inversely proportional to popularity, so low-popularity models receive higher weight in re-aggregation.

paras: Majority voting fails when multiple models make the same mistake together. This happens because models are not independent: a fine-tuned variant shares training data similarities with its parent, or multiple models studied the same web corpora and learned the same biases. When three models that were trained on overlapping data all vote red, majority voting treats it as strong evidence, but it is really one error repeated three times.

Here is the core mechanism: a model which disagrees with the crowd has already proven it does not share the crowd's correlated mistake. If Model X votes blue when everyone else votes red, and Model X is not in the main cluster, then Model X's blue vote is independent evidence. By upweighting such models, the algorithm trades away conformist redundancy for rare, uncorrelated signals. In domains with data bias (medical imaging, question answering), the low-popularity models are often the ones that caught a blind spot the majority missed.

The Optimal Weight variant adds a second layer: it also measures per-model accuracy on a side validation set. Models that are both independently-minded (low popularity) and individually accurate get the highest weight. Models that conform but are individually accurate get medium weight. Conformist, inaccurate models get low weight. This combines two dimensions of reliability into a single vote multiplier.

stages.s: All models answer the question independently
Compute majority consensus (what did most models say?)
For each model, measure: do they agree or buck the consensus?
Assign inverse weight: rebels get boosted, conformists get dampened
Re-aggregate votes using learned weights (optional: also measure individual accuracy)
Final answer, now resilient to correlated errors

math.words: For each model i, compute popularity as the fraction of questions where model i agrees with the majority. Then assign weight as one divided by popularity. The final answer is computed as the answer that has the highest sum of weights across all models that voted for it.
math.equation:
w_i = 1 / popularity_i, where popularity_i = (count of agreements with majority) / (total questions)
final_answer = argmax_a sum_i w_i * [model_i voted for a]
symbols: the weight given to model i's vote
the fraction of times model i agreed with the majority consensus
indicator: 1 if model i chose answer a, 0 otherwise
the answer option that accumulates the highest total weight

worked.title: A tiny worked example with four models and one new question
lines: Setup: On 10 prior questions, Model A always agreed with majority (popularity_A = 10/10 = 1.0, weight_A = 1/1.0 = 1.0).
Setup: Model B agreed 8 times (popularity_B = 8/10 = 0.8, weight_B = 1/0.8 = 1.25).
Setup: Model C agreed 4 times (popularity_C = 4/10 = 0.4, weight_C = 1/0.4 = 2.5).
Setup: Model D agreed 3 times (popularity_D = 3/10 = 0.3, weight_D = 1/0.3 = 3.33).
New question: Models A, B, C vote Red (3 votes). Model D votes Blue (1 vote).
Majority says Red (3 vs 1). But Model D is a rebel.
Red total weight: 1.0 + 1.25 + 2.5 = 4.75 (includes the consistent rebel C).
Blue total weight: 3.33 (the rare rebel D).

Majority voting picks Red. Weighted voting also picks Red, but notices the dissent. If D is right, the weight difference (4.75 vs 3.33) narrows the margin, allowing the algorithm to recover faster on future cases where the rebels are correct.

math.note: Each model's vote is multiplied by its weight, which is high for rebels and low for conformists, so independent minority answers get a louder voice.

charts.title: Majority voting (naive)
charts.note: Majority voting, unable to detect correlated errors, performs below the best individual model.

charts.title: ISP (Inverse Surprising Popularity)
charts.note: By upweighting rebels, ISP breaks through correlated errors and lifts the collective accuracy.

items.b: If all models are the same, there are no rebels.
items.html: If all ten models are the exact same fine-tuned variant, they will all have high popularity and all get equal weight. The algorithm collapses to majority voting, which is correct but uninteresting. The method works best when models are diverse.

items.b: If the validation set is biased, weights are wrong.
items.html: The popularity measurement is computed on a specific batch of test questions. If that batch has different bias than the deployment data, the weight assignments will be misleading. A model with low popularity on the validation set might actually be wrong in production.

Upweighting independent models assumes their dissent reveals a blind spot. But sometimes they are just wrong. If three models vote blue and seven vote red, and all three blues are actually incorrect, boosting them hurts accuracy. The method works well when the minority catches real gaps; it fails when the minority is simply inferior.

The method works best when models are trained on different data, use different architectures, or are fine-tuned with different objectives—so that their mistakes are truly independent. In that regime, rebels are gold.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: The demo should show that on a dataset where models have correlated errors (e.g., several models trained on overlapping data), weighted aggregation outperforms majority voting, especially on edge cases where the minority was right. This works because the upweighting mechanism gives more vote power to the independent models, so when they dissent, their vote has enough weight to flip the final decision. A concrete setup: fine-tune the same base model three different ways, each picking up a different data bias. Ask all three plus two independent models to answer questions on a holdout set. Mark questions where the correlated trio all agree vs questions where one of the independents disagrees. Run both majority voting and ISP on these questions and compare accuracy, focusing on the disagreement cases.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy_lift = (accuracy_ISP on disagreement cases) - (accuracy_majority_vote on disagreement cases)
demo.closing: The demo must show a case where the majority all agree and would pick wrong, but the low-popularity model picks right, and ISP correctly flips the final decision.
